replies.author: de0u
replies.text:
DavidXanatos Microsoft Word, Google Doc, LibreOffice Writer, etc., all have spell checkers. Another option might be writing in German and using a translator app. An ongoing problem with general-purpose LLMs is that, unless one is extremely careful about checking the output, plausible-seeming junk will creep in. In May, Anthropic's lawyers were in hot water because one of them asked Claude (Anthropic's LLM!) to properly format a legal citation to a real scientific paper, and instead it provided a citation for a paper that never existed (source).

If one has the knowledge and time and patience to carefully check every word that comes out of an LLM, they can be useful, but at present the key thing to know is that they are fundamentally unreliable.

mpn This happens to my dad: he suggested a business idea ...

Actually, open weight models including small ones you can run on your own device has the exact same problem. The term "sycophancy" is used by those deep into the LLM community to describe this behavior. Basically, LLMs are overtly ready to confirm and reinforce any idea you present, however detached from reality, and flattering you for coming up with the idea. The term "AI induced psychosis" has been used to describe the effect this behavior has on us.

The problem is thought to be an unintended side-effect of the RLHF (reinforcement learning through human feedback) phase during model post-training. It is likely not intended by the model creators. Yet, the problem has been known for a few years, and little progress has been made to stop the behavior.

This behavior is not thought to be a problem when using LLMs for purely software development, or for role-playing, but may be problematic when LLMs are being used as sounding boards or life coaches, which many do.

Before that social media was fringe, no reason to study it, and after that everyone used it, but no research had been done about possible negative consequences, including negative health consequences, of social media use. Today we know just how bad that is, and in which ways. Some believed the companies behind major social media networks were specifically tuning their algorithms to maximize engagement, and that this contributed to the poor mental health and exploitative behavior among social media users, and to a certain degree they did, but then people created free and open source social medias like Mastodon and friends, where anyone could see there is nothing nefarious in the algorithms, and yet, they were just as bad, and in the same ways, sometimes even worse. It is simply that kind of algorithms and platforms to begin with that has negative health effects.

Now we are seeing a rapid rise in the popularity of LLMs. No one has cared about LLMs before for the 20 years or so they have existed, and then suddenly a few years ago, and now everyone uses them. There hasn't been any reason to study what negative consequences there could be of LLM use before this, it was just a fringe community of role players who used them before. And here we are, and everyone uses them, and we barely understands what negative consequences LLM use may have, including negative health effects.

Maybe in 10 years we will know, and know well, I just find it a bit unfortunate that new technologies gets hyped and adopted this quickly. But I do believe that even if some commercial vendors of LLMs will manipulate responses in a way that is unacceptable, like social media companies did, most negative health effects and societal effects of LLM usage will be just as bad from open weight ones. And it is unclear right now whether it is an inherent flaw in the technology itself, like it seems to be with social medias, or whether the behavior can be "trained away". Only time will tell.

replies.author: rjo12
replies.text:
de0u

I don't really agree on that.

The advance in the "Attention is all you need" paper was essentially a change in the approach for how weights in a recursive neural network are computed. It reduced biasing of weights (e.g. when scanning a sentence, giving significantly less weight to words at the beginning than at the end) and is also suited to parallelism (which allows faster training of models with more parameters).

However, the problems of what are now described as hallucination and lying existed - and showed up regularly in experiments, albeit under different names - with machine learning approaches since the 1940s (at least). Those concerns tended to be played down by advocates - including researchers - who were pushing for wider acceptance and adoption of machine learning. The systems have been described as "intelligent" (the name "Artificial Intelligence" itself was, originally, conceived to encourage adoption, not to describe the actual system capability). There has also been regular pooh-poohing of concerns raised about assurance and safety of systems which take inputs from machine learning engines - for example, to autonomously control a vehicle or a weapon. Instead, the focus of research has been on getting the various machine learning approaches to better mimic behaviour of an intelligent system, rather than actually to BE an intelligent system.

All that's happened since 2017 is that very large commercial interests have gotten into the act. The advance of AI is now subject to commercial pressures prioritising the pushing of new product/features/models out the door rather than QA (so end users get to experience consequences the bugs, rather than them being found and squashed before release). The marketing push has increased, so the systems are presented as intelligent rather than as (advanced) mimics. Somehow, it is now viewed as appropriate to run experiments without safeguards on key production systems, or even on the internet, rather than on dedicated air-gapped (even if large) systems where the scope and consequences of any misbehaviours can be constrained, better understood, and (if the system is to be more widely deployed) managed. Doing a large scale cyber attack on a competitor is also now viewed as an appropriate marketing strategy, rather than as a criminal act or (if done by a government to systems owned by another nation) as potentially an act of war.

What hasn't changed is that these systems offer significant advances in capability, but also significant risks if they are deployed - deliberately or accidentally - without appropriate safeguards.

replies.author: GrapheneOS
replies.text: Jgmag1 Posting AI generated text in our forum, chat rooms and other community platforms is what's against the rules. There's no rule against people using it themselves but we strongly recommend people against credulously believing the output of LLMs. Even the latest frontier models go along with what people say and tell them what they want to hear. If you ask it to choose between 2 alternatives, it will keep going back between them if you disagree to always agree with you. What kind of source of information always tells you what you want to hear? This still applies even to using GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, etc. You should be very skeptical about their output and bear in mind they're largely basing it on consensus of their training data and dynamic sources. They're great at making highly inaccurate information look as if it's a very convincing expert written text. That's what they've been optimized to do. It's a very dangerous tool for people who don't deeply understand this.
